summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.

In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people face identity-document mismatch that drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition in Mexico depends on the state a person is in.

Tabasco has no legal gender-recognition procedure, according to Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion (6 March 2024). Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Context includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and the fact that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. Trans people in Tabasco live without documents that match their gender.

Mexico City has operated the longest-standing sub-national recognition regime. Amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code took effect on 13 March 2004 allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier to change gender on birth certificates; the legislature approved that measure 37-17 in late August 2008, formalising the procedure and replacing a prior process lacking specific rules that could take years in court. On 13 November 2014 the Legislative Assembly of Mexico City approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler.

Other states have legislated recognition procedures on their own timelines: the Michoacan Congress approved a gender identity law on 13 July 2017, Nayarit's on 20 July 2017, Coahuila passed a gender identity bill on 13 November 2018, the Hidalgo Congress approved a law on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosi began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019.

On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

Private same-sex sexual conduct between adults ceased to be a criminal matter in 1871 through adoption of the Napoleonic Code. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003 creating a national council to enforce it, and Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination, with the term sexual orientation inserted in June 2011. Mexico City passed an anti-discrimination ordinance covering sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first of its kind in the country.

Marriage recognition has been extended nationwide: Mexico City passed same-sex marriage on 21 December 2009 with effect on 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010; on 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court issued a jurisprudential thesis deeming marriage restrictions to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring judges to validate such unions through amparo, with nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalised on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.

Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatan Mayas, with Zapotecs recognizing a traditional third gender known as muxe, intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women's and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck. Although perceived as different from the general heterosexual male population, muxes are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities, though mestizo police occasionally harass muxe boys, prompting Zapotec parents to defend their right to be themselves.

Visible and well-attended LGBTQ marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.
tangentialFactors:
Impunity is the backdrop against which document mismatch and violence interact: more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, which bears directly on whether a trans person who faces violence while seeking documents or services can expect investigation.

The uneven patchwork of state procedures means a trans visitor's experience of document scrutiny can differ sharply between states, with Tabasco and Guanajuato recording incidents of discrimination tied to identity-document mismatch while Mexico City has operated a formal recognition procedure since 2004.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Tabasco live without documents matching their gender, which excludes them from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation.

Trans residents in the six states with no enacted procedure, and in the two operating one only in practice, lack a legislated route to recognition; only seven states extend recognition to children, affecting trans minors.

Residents of Mexico City, Michoacan, Nayarit, Coahuila, Hidalgo and San Luis Potosi have legislated gender-recognition procedures adopted between 2004 and 2019.

The August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa, Tabasco, occurred in a state with no recognition procedure and within a national homicide impunity rate above 95% in 2022.

Muxe identity among Isthmus Zapotecs carries community standing and familial pride, though mestizo police harassment of muxe boys is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that incidents of document-mismatch discrimination were recorded in Guanajuato is carried by the source inventory without specific dates or case details; the underlying incidents are not independently sourced here.

The inventory does not resolve whether the two states operating recognition procedures without legislative enactment have formal published rules or discretionary administrative practice.

The Supreme Court's 2018 holding and 2022 guidelines are described at a summary level; the specific binding force on states that have not legislated a procedure is not further documented in this inventory.
